doc.title: Manny Albam interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Adding strings to rock bands' tracks; the Beatles and George Martin
summary: He sweetened tracks for The Guess Who and others, then discusses the Beatles and George Martin.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: You seem to have certainly survived the rock & roll onslaught. Did it change your work at all when rock & roll became the popular music? © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-

Well what happened to me a couple of times, there used to be a group in Canada called The Guess Who. And there was another one called the Lloyds of London. They would come down to New York and cut a basic track and then I would go in and add strings and horns and whatever. And that began to become like a joke. They’d go in, first the bass player would come in and play his line. And then the guitar player came in and says, “wait a minute I can’t play with that thing, you’ve got G natural and it’s the wrong – I can’t do that.” So the bass player would have to make another track. And then the piano player came in and they’d change — so to get one thing down sometimes took three or four days. Finally they got two tracks down and I took them home and I would write “sweetening” is what they’d call it — strings and horns and all that. And we’d call the session and the string players came in and sat down and they played the thing through once and we recorded them the second time and they left and then the horn players came in. And these guys were, “holy Jesus, you mean you did the whole thing in 20 minutes? I can’t believe it.” I said, “well they’re musicians. They read music.” And after a while, I mean it paid but —
It’s taking money under false pretenses.
Really. After working with the guys on these things.

Some of the guys would come in and be in the horn section. You’d have like Marvin Stamm or Bill Watrous or whatever. They’d just come in, sit down and go [scats] and leave, and pick up their 90 dollars or whatever. And the groups didn’t know then who they were dealing with yet. They were dealing with great players. Jerome Richardson. These guys were — they had no idea. So God bless them. My kids love the Beatles. You know you can’t do anything about that. I like them, especially towards the end when they started getting arrangements. So I was sort of impressed by some of the groups that were at least musical in a way, went beyond the three chords. I loved that “Yellow Submarine,” that movie. It was a great thing.

Yeah. George Martin was the guy that really — I had a lot of admiration for, because he knew what he was doing and he convinced them that he was doing the right thing. So anyway, I don’t have any kind of anger about rock & roll. I’ll go along with it. But I don’t like to hear it when I pull up to a red light and all I hear is a bass line coming out of the car next to me. That’s something else.
